Hi Sandeep — thanks, we appreciate the clarity on what you need. High-level answers below and attached artifacts; technical deep-dive follows in a separate message from our runtime team (cc'd).

Key commitments (summary)
- Orchestration: Redwood executes a coordinated cutover using our control-plane orchestrator. For Hosted customers we can perform the DNS change (via pre-authorized change window) or hand the DNS swap to you — we recommend Redwood perform it for deterministic timing. Cutover is staged: drain -> final sync -> traffic shift -> post-checks. Typical time to shift (for Tidal-like workloads) is 6–12 minutes for warm-standby config, 2–4 minutes for active-active.
- KV cache & sessions: In-flight LLM sessions are kept in a combination of ephemeral KV cache (GPU-resident) and durable prefix store (S3-backed). We guarantee best-effort replay for partially completed sessions; fully persisted checkpoints (model state saved to durable storage) drive RPO. Expect a 0–30s potential loss window for warm-standby; for strict-zero-loss we recommend active-active with synchronous prefix replication.
- RTO/RPO signals: RTO is measured from incident declared -> successful request acknowledgment on new region (monitoring hooks + synthetic probes). RPO is measured by the timestamp of last persisted checkpoint in durable storage. We provide logs showing last-commit timestamps, replication lag, and request-gap graphs.

Attachments shared: redwood_drb_readiness_matrix_v1.xlsx, runbook-sample-snippet.pdf, arch-deployment-cache-warmup.png

On Fri, Jul 20, 2028 at 10:05 AM PDT Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com> wrote:
> Hi Sandeep — thanks, we appreciate the clarity on what you need. High-level answers below...

Hi Sandeep — adding the runtime-level detail you asked for so your infra team can validate assumptions. I'll keep this focused on the technical behaviors you will most likely test.

1) Cutover orchestration steps (technical sequence)\- Pre-cutover: health map + KV warmup plan seeded from durable prefix store (we compute a weighted key list driven by recent request traces).\- Drain: we stop accepting new sessions to the primary pool and mark connections STALED for graceful completion; existing token-generation completes or is checkpointed depending on policy.\- Final sync: any pending checkpointed session state is flushed to durable store; object-storage replication is verified (md5s/ETags).\- Switch: route-controller flips traffic (BGP or DNS, depending on plan). For DNS swaps we pre-create low-TTL DNS records; TTL propagation testing is part of rehearsal.\- Post-checks: synthetic queries, object-store consistency verification, and model warmup probes.

2) KV cache behavior and bounds
- Primary cache: GPU-local KV with TTLs; not durable across instance failure. We rely on the prefix store to refill cache after cutover.
- Warm-standby: partial state is available in a read-replica; warmup reduces cold-start penalty but introduces modest RPO (typ. seconds).
- Active-active: we support near-synchronous replication for prefix/durable stores; this is the recommended configuration for sub-second RPOs.

3) Session affinity and client-side sticky sessions
- We recommend token-based session affinity (client attaches session token to requests). On cutover, a short-lived token mapping table is used to resolve new region mapping to resume in-flight sessions where possible. Full continuity depends on whether you require GPU-resident cache rehydration vs replay from prefix store.

4) Operational signals (what we expose)
- Replication lag (ms/sec)
- Last persisted checkpoint timestamp (ISO)
- Synthetic probe RTT and success rate
- Cache-warmup progress (keys loaded / total)

5) Rehearsal playbook highlights
- Run one dry rehearsal, then one live rehearsal on low-traffic window. Each rehearsal produces a checklist-based report (time-to-dns, time-to-first-successful-probe, replication-lag chart). We attach those artifacts post-run.

If Tidal's infra team wants, we can instrument a short-lived agent in your staging to record TTL effects and measure DNS propagation in your client network.

—Vivek

Soojin / Vivek — thanks for the detailed notes. A couple of clarifications from the infra side before we schedule:

- For active-active synchronous prefix replication, what is the expected write amplification and how does that affect token-generation latency? We need numbers or a test harness to validate our 99th pct CPU budget.
- During the drain step you mention sessions can be "checkpointed" — are checkpoints created synchronously inline with the request or asynchronously? We need to understand the extra latencies introduced.
- TTLs on GPU-resident KV: if we see hot keys with sub-second TTLs, does Redwood offer an in-flight prefetch or pinning mechanism to avoid repeated repopulation after cutover?

Alex — great questions, and all answerable. Quick responses and commitments below, we'll follow up with a short technical appendix and a small test harness we can run in your staging (to surface numbers).

- Write amplification / latency: for synchronous prefix replication in our active-active profile we typically observe a write amplification of ~1.2–1.6x for small checkpoint objects; median extra latency 6–12ms, 99th pct depends on region interconnect (we'll supply measured numbers from prior tests). The staging harness will produce 95/99/99.9 pct histograms for your workload.
- Checkpointing model: by default checkpoints are created asynchronously to avoid adding tail latency to token generation; we provide an option for inline synchronous checkpointing if you require stronger durability (with the latency trade-off documented).
- Hot-key pinning: we support an in-flight pin API (server-side) for short-lived hot keys and a proactive prefetch policy during warmup that pins selected keys until the rehydration window completes. We'll include a sample config you can use.

Rehearsal confirmation: Redwood confirms both windows. We will need a one-hour pre-auth for DNS swap if Redwood performs the change; if Tidal prefers to perform the swap we will provide the exact TTL/DNS records and run pre-checks. We'll create a shared folder with the rehearsal checklist and invite your infra SSO identities.

2) Tidal to confirm whether Redwood is authorized for DNS swap or if the swap will be performed by Tidal.
